title: Cain and Abel: The First Murder
summary: Eve bears two sons, Cain the farmer and Abel the shepherd. When God accepts Abel's offering and not Cain's, Cain grows angry, ignores God's warning about sin crouching at his door, and kills his brother. God sends Cain out as a wanderer but marks him for protection. Cain's line builds a city and invents herding, music, and metalwork, and it produces Lamech, who boasts of vengeance; meanwhile a new son, Seth, is born, and people begin to call on the name of the LORD.
story: Outside Eden, life goes on. The first birth is greeted with hope, and the first act of worship follows. But the sin that began with a question in the garden now grows into murder within a single generation. Chapter 3 broke the bond between people and God; chapter 4 shows how that break spreads sideways, into the bond between brothers. The chapter then traces two lines. Cain's descendants build civilization and grow more violent, while Seth's line begins quietly with worship. That contrast sets up the genealogy of chapter 5 and the flood that will come when violence fills the earth.
historical:
Like the chapters before it, this one belongs to the early history of humanity that Genesis tells without dates. It gives the origin of three ways of life that every ancient reader knew: the tent-dwelling herdsman, the musician with harp and pipe, and the smith who works bronze and iron. Mesopotamian tradition told of seven wise beings from before the flood, the apkallu, who brought the arts of civilization to humankind from the gods. Genesis credits those same kinds of achievements to ordinary human beings, and to the line of a murderer. Culture is a human work, capable of great good, and it is not holy in itself.

The mention of bronze and iron is worth a note. Bronze was worked widely in the Near East from the fourth and third millennia BC, while iron came into common use only around 1200 BC, though smaller iron objects are known from much earlier. The verse is not trying to date the invention. It names the metals a later reader knew and traces the craft back to the earliest generations.
cultural:
The two brothers represent the two great ways of making a living in the ancient Near East, farming and herding, which often lived in tension. Their offerings follow their work: Cain brings produce, Abel brings the firstborn of the flock and the best portions, literally the fat, which Israel's later law reserved for God. Offerings of grain were perfectly acceptable in Israel's law, so the difference is not simply plants versus animals. The text contrasts some of Cain's fruit with the choicest and first of Abel's flock, and then shows Cain's heart in his anger.

In the ancient world, blood that was shed unjustly was thought to demand an answer, and the next of kin was expected to avenge a murder. Cain's fear that whoever finds him will kill him reflects that world of blood feud. God's mark on Cain is a sign of protection, not of shame, and it limits the violence. Lamech turns that protection inside out, boasting to his wives that he has killed a young man for wounding him and will take vengeance seventy-sevenfold. He is also the first man in the Bible with two wives. Within a few generations the line of Cain has moved from one murder with remorse to killing as a matter for poetry.
literary: The chapter is built on echoes of chapter 3. God's question to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” (verse 9), mirrors his question to Adam, and his second question, “What have you done?” (verse 10), mirrors his question to Eve. Cain, like his parents, is driven out, east of Eden. The warning in verse 7 uses the same words as 3:16: sin's desire is for Cain, and he must rule over it. Irony runs through the story. Cain answers God with a question, “Am I my brother's keeper?” (verse 9), using the same verb, to keep or guard, that described Adam's charge in the garden. The ground that was cursed now opens its mouth to drink blood. The last part of the chapter shifts to genealogy and closes with Lamech's short poem, the first recorded song after the fall, and a brief new beginning with Seth and Enosh.

outline.t: Two offerings and a warning about sin
Cain kills Abel and is sent away
The mark of Cain and the land of Nod
Cain's line: city, crafts, and Lamech's song of vengeance
Seth is born, and people call on the LORD

doctrines.note: The first time the Bible uses the word sin, it pictures it as something crouching at the door, eager to master a person who must instead master it. The chapter shows sin as a power that grows: envy becomes anger, anger becomes murder, murder becomes a boast. It also shows that people remain responsible; God speaks to Cain before the crime and calls him to choose.

Abel's blood cries out from the ground, and God hears it. Human life is precious to God even when no one else is watching, and violence against a brother is violence God answers. Cain's line also shows the human capacity for culture, art, and skill, gifts that remain good even in a broken world.

God judges Cain by sending him away from the ground and from his presence, yet he also protects him from being killed in turn. Judgment and mercy come together, and God keeps the right of vengeance to himself rather than leaving it to blood feud.

The chapter ends with the first mention of people calling on the name of the LORD, the Bible's language for public worship and prayer. Amid the spread of violence, a line of people who turn to God begins.

words.note: Chattat, sin. This is the word's first appearance in the Bible. Its basic idea is missing the mark or failing, and it later also names the sin offering. Here it is pictured almost as a living thing lying in wait at the door. Some scholars compare a Mesopotamian image of a demon that lurks at a threshold, which suits the vivid picture of sin crouching and desiring.

Hevel, the name Abel. As an ordinary word it means breath, vapor, or something fleeting, the word that runs through Ecclesiastes and is often translated vanity or meaningless. The narrator never comments on the name, but a Hebrew reader would feel it: the brother whose life vanished like a breath.

Qanah, to acquire, get, or produce, which Eve uses at Cain's birth (translated I have brought forth). The verb sounds like Cain's name, Qayin. Eve's words have been read as joy at God's help in giving life after the fall, and some have heard hope that this son might be the promised seed, a hope his life cruelly disappoints.

Ot, sign or mark. The same word is used for the rainbow in 9:12-13, for circumcision in 17:11, and for the blood on Israel's doorposts at Passover. The text never says what Cain's mark looked like. Its purpose is what matters: it is a sign of God's protection over a guilty man.

christ: The New Testament returns to this chapter several times. Jesus speaks of “the blood of righteous Abel” as the first in a long line of innocent blood (Matthew 23:35). Hebrews says that “By faith Abel offered God a better sacrifice than Cain did” (Hebrews 11:4), and later sets the blood of Jesus beside Abel's: we have come “to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24). Abel's blood cried out for justice; Christ's blood speaks forgiveness. John holds up Cain as the pattern of hatred between brothers and contrasts it with the love Christ shows (1 John 3:11-16). And when Peter asks whether he should forgive seven times, Jesus answers, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:22). In the Greek translation of Genesis the number matches Lamech's boast, and many readers see Jesus deliberately turning Lamech's limitless vengeance into limitless forgiveness.

hard.q: Where did Cain's wife come from, and who was Cain afraid of?
hard.a:
The chapter mentions Cain's wife and a city full of people without saying where they came from, and Cain fears that whoever finds him will kill him. The oldest and most common answer, found already in ancient Jewish tradition, is that Adam and Eve had many children (5:4 mentions other sons and daughters), that Cain married a sister or niece, and that the population grew quickly over long lifespans. On this view the story names only the people who matter to the plot, and marriage between close relatives had not yet been forbidden, as it would be in Israel's law (Leviticus 18).

Others argue that the chapter itself seems to assume a wider human population, and they take this as a sign that Genesis 2 to 4 is not trying to give a complete census. Some who read Adam and Eve as a real couple chosen from among early humans hold this view, as do those who read the chapters as a representative story about humanity. Both groups agree that the narrator's interest lies elsewhere, in what sin does between brothers and how God responds.

questions: God warns Cain that sin is crouching at his door before he acts. What warning signs do you tend to ignore when anger or envy begins to take hold?
Cain asks, Am I my brother's keeper? How would you answer that question for your own family, church, or neighborhood?
Cain's descendants build cities and invent music and tools, yet violence grows alongside them. How can a culture be skilled and creative and still be moving away from God?
